clue.text: Edit traced out

indicators.note: something put out of place is knocked out of order, so the letters must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: 'Traced out' reads like a description of drawing over lines; 'out' is only the signal to rearrange the six letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To redact a text is to prepare it for publication, often by censoring passages, which is a kind of editing.

clue.text: Regret some tremors eventually

indicators.note: 'some' asks for only a portion of what follows, a run of letters spanning the words

parts.note: the run starts after the first letter and ends at the first letter of the second word

explanation.surface: Someone feels sorry about a run of earth tremors that finally came.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the leading T of 'tremors' and borrow the E that starts 'eventually'.
explanation.definitionFit: Remorse is deep regret or guilt for a wrong committed, so the two nouns are close synonyms.

clue.text: Singer revealed by body language to some extent

indicators.note: what is revealed by something is uncovered inside it, showing a run of letters within
only partly, so a portion of the following words is all that is wanted

parts.note: the tail of the first word joined to the start of the second

explanation.surface: A performer's feelings show partly through their gestures and posture.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters straddle the gap between 'body' and 'language'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob Dylan is the famous American singer-songwriter, so the answer is an example of a singer.

clue.text: Get rid of money — that is right

parts.note: a straightforward synonym
i.e. is the abbreviation of Latin id est, 'that is'
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone decides to throw away their money, and insists that is the correct thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer looks like the bank clerk, but here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To cashier someone is to dismiss them from service, especially an officer from the armed forces, in disgrace.

clue.text: Special hats making mister daft

indicators.note: silly or crazy, so the letters are scrambled into a mad new order

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Wearing silly hats makes a gentleman look foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daft' seems to describe the mister, but it only tells you to rearrange his six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A mitre is the tall pointed ceremonial headdress worn by bishops, a particular kind of hat for church occasions.

clue.text: Six-footer in religious group?

parts.note: taken as written
a sect is a religious faction

explanation.surface: A very tall person belongs to some religious community.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six-footer' suggests a tall person, but it means a creature with six feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Insects have six legs, so every one is literally a creature with six feet, a playful description.

clue.text: Recount a bit of rigmarole funnily? I may!

definitions.text: Recount a bit of rigmarole funnily? I may!

indicators.note: done in a funny or odd way, so the letters are arranged strangely

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a bit is a small part, so only the opening letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the first letter

explanation.surface: A storyteller admits they might relate a long rambling tale in a humorous way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recount a' plus R are the letters to shuffle; read as a whole, the clue is the answer speaking about itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A raconteur is a skilled teller of anecdotes, exactly someone who might amusingly recount a rambling yarn.

clue.text: The female has been a boozer!

parts.note: the female pronoun
the past participle, with 'has' as grammar

explanation.surface: An accusation that a woman used to be a heavy drinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A boozer' suggests a drunkard, but in British slang a boozer is also a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A shebeen is an unlicensed drinking den, originally Irish, so it is a kind of pub or drinking place.

clue.text: Thoughts of the French about being made free

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: French for 'of the' with a plural noun
the act of setting free

explanation.surface: French ideas concerning emancipation.
explanation.walkthrough: DES is split, its S landing at the end after the inserted word.
explanation.definitionFit: Deliberations are careful considerations or reflections, which are a form of thoughts on a subject.

clue.text: German boy taking green fruit around

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a lime is a green citrus fruit

explanation.surface: A German lad is carrying unripe fruit about with him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green fruit' suggests unripe, but it is a fruit that is green.
explanation.definitionFit: Emil is a common German male given name, so it serves as an example of a German boy.

clue.text: Material produced by two people: one wise, the other foolish

parts.note: a seer is a prophet, a wise visionary
a sucker is a gullible fool

explanation.surface: Some fabric is made by a pair, one sage and one fool.
explanation.walkthrough: The two people are the two halves of the answer: a prophet followed by a dupe.
explanation.definitionFit: Seersucker is a puckered, striped cotton fabric used for summer clothing, a kind of cloth.

clue.text: British character of old coming to one sultanate

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
a rune is a letter of an ancient alphabet
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned British personality arrives in a sultan's realm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' looks like a person, but it is a written character, an old letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Brunei is a small state on Borneo ruled by a sultan, so it is an instance of a sultanate.

clue.text: Nice dens made special with perfume

indicators.note: something specially made is crafted afresh, so the letters are reworked into a new form

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Pleasant rooms are given a special touch with fragrance.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer usually means furious; here it is read as filled with incense.
explanation.definitionFit: Incensed in its literal sense means scented with burning incense, so perfumed by fragrant smoke.

clue.text: French thinker upsetting sacred set

indicators.note: to upset is to overturn and disturb, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A French philosopher offends a group of devout believers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upsetting' seems to be what the philosopher does to believers; it is the signal to rearrange the two words after it.
explanation.definitionFit: René Descartes was the seventeenth-century French philosopher of 'I think, therefore I am'.

clue.text: See building

parts.note: surface reading: an instruction to go and look at some building; setter's reading: the principal church of a bishop's see, or diocese

explanation.walkthrough: 'See' reads as a verb; it is the noun meaning a bishop's diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedral contains the bishop's throne and is the main church of his diocese, the building of a see.

clue.text: Sound of stream in foreign capital

indicators.note: the sound of a word is how it is spoken, so a word that is said the same is wanted

parts.note: a burn is a Scottish and northern English word for a small stream

explanation.surface: The gurgle of a brook is heard in a city abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The stream is a Scottish burn, and the capital is spelt differently but sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Bern is the capital city of Switzerland, so to a British setter it is a capital abroad.

clue.text: Quaint fashion, latest in Vogue

parts.note: the cut of a garment is its style

indicators.note: the latest of something is the last to come, so the final letter is taken

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned style is the newest thing in the fashion magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Vogue is the fashion magazine, which helps the surface, but only its last letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Quaint means charmingly old-fashioned or attractively unusual, close to sweet or appealing in a dainty way.

clue.text: Firm dad keeping quiet in officers' HQ

parts.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company, a firm

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece holds another inside

parts.note: pop is an informal word for father
the sound used to ask for quiet

explanation.surface: A strict father keeps silent inside the officers' headquarters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like an adjective describing dad, but it is a business.
explanation.definitionFit: Cop shop is slang for a police station, the base where police officers work.

clue.text: Type of dish — cereal's so different

indicators.note: made different means changed in form, so the letters take a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on a kind of dish that breakfast cereal is quite unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'cereal's' is ignored; its S joins the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A casserole is both a deep oven pot and the slow-cooked stew made in it, so a kind of dish.

clue.text: Second request for watering device?

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a prayer is a humble request

explanation.surface: Asking a second time for something to water the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second request' looks like asking again, but 'second' is just its abbreviation, put in front of the request.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprayer is an appliance that disperses liquid in droplets, used for watering plants in a garden.

clue.text: Erudite king meeting Scottish lout?

parts.note: King Lear, Shakespeare's tragic king
a ned is a Scottish slang word for a young hooligan

explanation.surface: A scholarly monarch has an encounter with a Glasgow yob.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Lear is the crossword's favourite king, and a ned is a Scottish young troublemaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone having great knowledge gained through study, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Report of a certain coming to land

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the spoken form is wanted

parts.note: 'a sure' is 'a certain', and in many British accents it is said the same

explanation.surface: News arrives that a particular person is making landfall.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'a sure' with a British non-rhotic accent and it matches the answer; 'certain' and 'sure' are synonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashore means onto the land from the water, as in going towards the shore from a boat.

clue.text: Party with a group of journalists — kids, not half!

indicators.note: not half means only half survives, so the word is cut down the middle

parts.note: taken as written
the press is journalists collectively
the first half of the four-letter word, the second half dropped

explanation.surface: A celebration with reporters and their children, a really lively one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much so', but here it literally halves the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Après-ski is the socialising and partying at a ski resort after the day's skiing, a sort of party.

clue.text: Artist with face somehow beaming?

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician, is the usual crossword artist
a clock face is its dial, and dial is also slang for a person's face

explanation.surface: A painter has a face that is somehow smiling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beaming' suggests smiling; the question mark warns it means sending out beams.
explanation.definitionFit: Radial means spreading out from a centre like rays, so in a fashion it is like beams of light.

clue.text: Daughter meeting dissolute fellow — a flighty male

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter
a rake is a man of loose morals

explanation.surface: A girl takes up with a debauched man, an unreliable sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flighty' implies fickle, but here it is a male that can fly.
explanation.definitionFit: A drake is a male duck, a bird able to fly, so literally a male capable of flight.

clue.text: Fish starter for Spanish gent with no wine

parts.note: char is a fish of the trout family
Don is a Spanish title for a gentleman
nay is an old word for no

explanation.surface: A Spanish gentleman is served a fish course but no wine to go with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' suggests a first course; it only places the fish at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Chardonnay is a white grape variety and the dry white wine made from it.

clue.text: Girl making money in India once

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a common female name
second meaning: a former coin of India, a sixteenth of a rupee

explanation.surface: A young woman earned a living in colonial India.
explanation.walkthrough: The anna was a coin of British India, worth one sixteenth of a rupee.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a popular girl's name and also an old Indian coin, now no longer in circulation.

clue.text: Soft protection for the 'ead, a decorative piece

indicators.note: the apostrophe shows a dropped aitch, as in Cockney speech, so that letter must go

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for soft
a helmet protects the head; with the aitch dropped it loses its first letter

explanation.surface: A padded cap for the head is, in a Cockney voice, an ornamental item.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the H from 'head' is the hint to drop it from the headgear too.
explanation.definitionFit: A pelmet is an ornamental border fitted above a window to hide the curtain fixtures, a decorative piece.

clue.text: Chum got very hot around end of afternoon

indicators.note: going around something encloses it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: to fry in the heat, as in the sun

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, which is the one kept

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: A pal got sunburnt late in the afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter from the end of the afternoon goes inside 'fried', just before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Chum is informal for a close companion, so the two words are synonyms for a person you are fond of.
